summary:
Guaviare Department stands under Colombia's national legal framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds has been prohibited by statute since 2011, the Constitutional Court opened same-sex marriage in April 2016, and adoption by same-sex couples has been available since 2015. Legal gender recognition rests on Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993, and since June 2015 a trans Colombian changes the sex marker on government identification by signing a document before a notary rather than submitting to judicially ordered bodily or psychiatric examination. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

A national LGBTI policy text addresses rights in public education, health care, prisons and the status of victims of the armed conflict, and its victim-protection provisions engage directly with the risk pattern described below.

The violence a trans visitor faces is set at national scale. Reporting current to mid-2025 counts nearly 50 queer and trans people killed in Colombia that year to date; 41 trans people were killed in 2023, and eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024. One account counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone.

Impunity is the defining feature of that toll. Of 155 criminal investigations into LGBTQ killings, only three reached a verdict in the year covered by the reporting, a conviction rate of roughly 2 per cent against 9 per cent for homicides generally.

Armed groups operating despite the 2016 peace agreement drive the most acute risk. In Guajira, flyers posted from March 2024 carried kill lists of named individuals under wording that identified "homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans" as targets. In Caquetá, "social cleansing" flyers circulated on the street and through WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. Trans women in Caquetá reported few options beyond hairdressing or sex work, and Tatiana Cespedes, a 51-year-old trans woman, was told by three armed men that she had one week to leave town or be killed; after hiding for a week she fled at night.

Targeted killing is not confined to territories under armed-group control. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia in April 2025 and drowned after being beaten with fractured limbs; President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Some conflict-period violence has been prosecuted as an international crime: in July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging gender persecution as a crime against humanity.

No source in the current inventory reports a Guaviare-specific incident, facility, enforcement action or protection mechanism. The assessment for Guaviare is therefore the national pattern of armed-group threat and investigative failure, combined with the thin institutional reach characteristic of Colombia's smaller peripheral departments.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement gap separates a reformed legal baseline from daily experience. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, welcoming the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and lived experience are disconnected and that rising killings require urgent attention.

Violence takes two distinct forms that a visitor should not conflate. One is conflict-zone enforcement by armed groups through published kill lists and expulsion campaigns, documented in Caquetá and Guajira. The other is ordinary urban targeted killing, as in the April 2025 attack on Sara Millerey in Bello, near Medellín, where a video of the assault circulated widely and solidarity events followed in several cities. An "As Equals" investigation also traces the history of "social cleansing" campaigns and a gang alliance enforcing social order in the Medellín area, including the expulsion of gay and trans residents.

Economic marginalisation compounds exposure. Reporting from Caquetá found discrimination limiting trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, which concentrates them in settings where armed-group threats and police contact are more likely.

The pattern is not treated as ordinary homicide by the justice system in every instance. The July 2023 indictments by the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, and registered concern from the UN Human Rights Committee, place the same conduct within an international-crime framework that ordinary homicide proceedings do not reach.
localsOnly:
Resident trans Colombians change the sex marker on government identification by notarial act, a route available since June 2015 and grounded in Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognising legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

The national LGBTI policy text sets rights obligations in public education, health care, prisons and for victims of the armed conflict, and its victim-protection clause is the domestic instrument through which conflict-related targeting of LGBT people is meant to be addressed.

A comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025, so protections rest on constitutional jurisprudence, court rulings and administrative acts rather than a single statute.

Residents of departments where armed groups are present have been directly threatened in place: Caquetá residents received expulsion flyers on the street and by WhatsApp, and Guajira residents were named on posted kill lists from March 2024. Eight trans women were killed nationally between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports any Guaviare-specific incident, detention facility, health service, police practice or protection mechanism; the department entry consulted contains no usable jurisdiction-specific finding. The Guaviare assessment rests entirely on the national pattern and on the general observation that Colombia's smaller peripheral departments have thinner institutional reach, which is not itself sourced to a Guaviare study.

The conviction figures (3 of 155 investigations reaching a verdict) are attributed to "last year" in reporting dated 6 August 2025, and the underlying reporting year is not stated precisely in the available material; the near-50 and 41-kill totals are similarly anchored to the date of reporting rather than to a closed calendar year.

The national legal baseline is drawn from an encyclopaedic summary rather than primary legislation or court text, and the June 2015 notarial procedure, the November 2025 identification markers and the pending comprehensive trans law are restated from the parent-framework record rather than verified against the statute books in this pass.

Whether Guaviare's own police, prosecutor's office or municipal administrations have any LGBTI-specific protocol, complaint route or shelter is unresolved and not sourced.
